title: Poems and Plays
bigQuestion: How do poems and plays tell a story differently from a book, and what do you have to do to read them well?

story.title: The Drum Inside the Poem
story.kicker: The first time the class read the poem, it was just words. The second time, they heard hoofbeats.
paragraphs: Mr. Bell put four lines on the board. "Whenever the moon and stars are set, / Whenever the wind is high, / All night long in the dark and wet, / A man goes riding by." He asked Kenji to read them. Kenji read them the way he read everything: fast, flat, done. "Okay," said Mr. Bell. "Now we read it again. This time, listen for the drum."

"What drum?" said Kenji. Mr. Bell did not answer. He tapped the desk. Tap, TAP, tap, TAP. Then he read the first line, slow, letting his voice land hard on some words and light on others. "Whenever the MOON and STARS are SET." A few kids started tapping too. By the third line, the whole room was doing it.

"That," said Mr. Bell, "is a horse." The poem is about a rider who gallops past in the storm every night, and the poet built the sound of hooves right into the words. Robert Louis Stevenson wrote it more than a hundred years ago for a book of poems for children. He was a sick boy who spent a lot of nights awake, listening to the wind.

Kenji read the lines a third time, tapping as he went. This time he slowed down at "dark and wet" and sped up at "riding by." It sounded like a story. It sounded a little scary. "I didn't get that the first time," he said. "Nobody does," said Mr. Bell. "A poem is not finished until you hear it."

Then Mr. Bell handed out a one-page play with two parts, a rider and a child at a window. "Same night, same storm," he said. "But this time you are going to say the words out loud and be the people. That is the other thing we do with words on a page: we stand up and become them."
story.think: What changed between Kenji's first reading and his third? Why do you think a poem might need to be heard, not just seen?

lessons.title: Lines and Stanzas
lessons.mainIdea: A poem is built from lines, and lines are grouped into stanzas; where a line breaks is a choice the poet made.
reading: Look at a page of a story. The words run to the edge and wrap around. Now look at a poem. The words stop early, on purpose, and start again on the next line. Each row of a poem is a *line*. The poet decides where every line ends. That is the first thing that makes a poem look like a poem.

Lines are grouped into *stanzas*. A stanza is a chunk of lines with a space before and after it. It works a little like a paragraph. Each stanza often holds one picture or one step of the idea. When you reach the white space, pause. Something is about to shift.

Try this short poem, written for this lesson: "The bus is late. / The rain is cold. / My shoes are wet. / My socks are old." Four lines, one stanza. Each line is one small complaint, and the line breaks make you feel them one at a time. Written as a sentence, they would blur together. Broken into lines, each one lands.

words.d: one row of words in a poem, ending where the poet chose to stop
a group of lines in a poem, set off by blank space, like a paragraph

look.title: Same Words, Two Shapes
look.text: Version one: "The bus is late, the rain is cold, my shoes are wet, my socks are old." Version two: "The bus is late. / The rain is cold. / My shoes are wet. / My socks are old." Read each one out loud.
look.prompt: Which version sounds more tired and fed up? What do the line breaks do to the way you read it?

check.q: What is a stanza?
choices: A group of lines in a poem set off by blank space
The last line of a poem
check.why: A stanza is a chunk of lines, a bit like a paragraph.

check.q: Who decides where a poem's line ends?
check.why: Line breaks are the poet's choice, not an accident of the page.

check.q: What should you do when you reach the white space between stanzas?
check.why: Each stanza often holds one picture or step. The space is a signal to pause.

lessons.title: Rhythm and Rhyme
lessons.mainIdea: Rhythm is the beat made by stressed and unstressed syllables, and rhyme is matching sounds at the ends of lines.
reading: Say your own name and listen. One part is louder. KEN-ji. Ma-RI-a. Every word has beats, and some beats are stressed, or louder. A poet lines up stressed beats in a pattern, and that pattern is *rhythm*. It is the drum Mr. Bell's class heard: "whenEVer the MOON and STARS are SET."

*Rhyme* is a different tool. It is a match of sounds at the ends of lines. Set and wet. High and by. Cold and old. Rhyme makes lines stick together and makes a poem easy to remember. That is why songs and jump-rope chants rhyme. Not every poem rhymes, but when one does, you can hear the ends of the lines click shut.

You can find rhythm by tapping and rhyme by listening to the last word of each line. Try it on this: "I lost my hat, / I found my hat, / It's on the cat." Tap: the beat is steady, bump-BUMP-bump-BUMP. Listen: hat, hat, cat. Rhythm and rhyme together are why the poem sounds like a little song.

words.d: the beat of a poem, made by the pattern of louder and softer syllables
matching sounds at the ends of words, like set and wet
said louder or harder than the beats around it

look.title: Syllables in Four Lines of Windy Nights
rows: Whenever the moon and stars are set,
All night long in the dark and wet,
look.cite: counted for this lesson; lines by Robert Louis Stevenson, A Child's Garden of Verses, 1885
look.prompt: The lines get shorter toward the end of the stanza. Read them aloud. What does the short last line do to the sound of the rider?

check.q: What makes a poem's rhythm?
choices: The pattern of stressed and unstressed beats
check.why: Rhythm is the beat, made by which syllables get stressed.

check.q: Which pair rhymes?
check.why: High and by end with the same sound.

check.q: Why do so many songs and chants rhyme?
choices: Rhyme makes lines stick together and easy to remember
check.why: Matching sounds help words stay in your head.

lessons.title: Saying It Again
lessons.mainIdea: Poets repeat words, lines and sounds on purpose, and the repetition tells you what matters most.
reading: "Whenever the moon and stars are set, / Whenever the wind is high." Two lines in a row start with the same word. That is not a mistake. It is *repetition*, saying something again on purpose. Repeating "whenever" makes the storm feel like it comes again and again, every night.

Repetition works like a drumbeat you cannot ignore. Repeat a word and the reader notices it. Repeat a whole line and it becomes a *refrain*, like the chorus of a song. Songs use refrains because the part you hear most is the part you remember. Poems do the same thing.

Here is a tiny poem written for this lesson: "Wait for the bus. / Wait for the bell. / Wait for the light. / Wait for the tell-tale click of the door." The word wait comes four times. You feel the waiting. When a poet repeats something, ask what feeling the repeat is building. That feeling is usually close to the heart of the poem.

words.d: using the same word, line or sound more than once on purpose
a line or group of lines repeated in a poem or song, like a chorus

look.title: One Word, Over and Over
look.text: Wait for the bus. / Wait for the bell. / Wait for the light. / Wait for the tell-tale click of the door.
look.cite: model poem, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which word repeats? What feeling does the repetition build, and why is the last line longer?

check.q: What is repetition in a poem?
choices: A mistake the poet forgot to fix
Using the same word or line again on purpose
A rhyme at the end of a line
check.why: Poets repeat on purpose, to make you notice and feel the words.

check.q: A whole line that repeats in a poem or song is called a
check.why: A refrain is a repeated line, like a chorus.

check.q: In the model poem, what does repeating "wait" make you feel?
choices: The long slow feeling of waiting
check.why: Four waits in a row build the feeling of waiting itself.

lessons.title: Reading a Poem Aloud
lessons.mainIdea: A poem is meant to be heard, so read it aloud slowly, following the punctuation, not just the line ends.
reading: Kenji's first reading was fast and flat, and the poem stayed dead on the board. His third reading was slow, with taps, and the poem woke up. Reading a poem out loud is not a test of speed. It is how you find the sound the poet built into it.

Three rules help. First, slow down. A poem packs a lot into few words, so give each word room. Second, follow the *punctuation*, not the line ends. If a line has no period or comma at the end, keep going into the next line without a big stop. Third, let your voice rise and fall with the rhythm. Tap it out if that helps.

Fourth, and this one matters: read it more than once. The first time, just get the words. The second time, listen for the beat. The third time, try to sound like the poem feels: spooky, sleepy, excited, sad. Every time you *perform* a poem this way, you understand it better. That is not cheating. That is reading.

words.d: marks like periods and commas that tell a reader where to pause or stop
to read or act something out loud for others, with feeling

look.title: Where Does the Voice Stop?
look.text: Two lines from a poem written for this lesson: "The kite pulled hard against my hand / and then let go." There is no mark at the end of the first line. Read it with a full stop after hand. Now read it straight through, pausing only at the period.
look.prompt: Which reading matches what a kite does? Why should you follow the punctuation and not just the line end?

check.q: A line of a poem ends with no punctuation. What should your voice do?
choices: Keep moving into the next line
check.why: Follow the punctuation. No mark means no big stop.

check.q: Why read a poem more than once?
choices: Because the first reading is always wrong
Each reading finds something new: words, then beat, then feeling
check.why: First the words, then the rhythm, then the feeling. Each pass adds something.

check.q: What was wrong with Kenji's first reading?
choices: It was fast and flat, so the sound never showed
check.why: Fast and flat hides the drum. Slow and tapped brings it out.

lessons.title: Pictures Made of Words
lessons.mainIdea: Imagery is language that makes a picture, sound, smell, taste or touch in the reader's mind, using the five senses.
reading: "All night long in the dark and wet." You cannot see the storm, but you can feel it: dark, wet, cold, long. Words that make you see, hear, smell, taste or touch something are *imagery*. A poet uses imagery so you do not just read about the storm. You stand in it.

Imagery works through the five *senses*. Sight: a red kite against gray clouds. Sound: the slap of rain on the windows. Smell: wet dog. Taste: a mouthful of salt water. Touch: the scratch of a wool sweater. Good poets pick the one detail that puts you there. "It was a nice day" is not imagery. "The sidewalk burned through my flip-flops" is.

When you read a poem, hunt for the senses. Underline the words you can see. Circle the ones you can hear or feel. Then ask what the poet wanted you to notice most. A poem about summer that talks only about heat is telling you something. A poem about winter that mentions the smell of soup is telling you something else.

words.d: words that create a picture, sound, smell, taste or touch in the reader's mind
sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch: the five ways we take in the world

look.title: Wind You Cannot See
look.text: Who has seen the wind? / Neither I nor you: / But when the leaves hang trembling, / The wind is passing through.
look.prompt: The wind cannot be seen. Which word lets you see it anyway? Which sense is the poet using?

check.q: Which sentence uses imagery?
choices: The sidewalk burned through my flip-flops
check.why: Burned through my flip-flops makes you feel the heat. The others just tell.

check.q: What are the five senses?
check.why: Imagery reaches the reader through those five senses.

check.q: "The leaves hang trembling." Which sense does this reach?
check.why: You see the leaves shaking. That is how the poem shows the wind.

lessons.title: Words That Sound Like Sounds
lessons.mainIdea: Some words sound like the noise they name, and poets use them to put sound directly into a line.
reading: Buzz. Crash. Drip. Hiss. Say them out loud. Each one sounds like the thing it means. A word that imitates a sound is a *sound word*. The long name for it is onomatopoeia, which is hard to spell and fun to say. You already use sound words all the time: a dog goes woof, a clock goes tick.

Poets love sound words because they do two jobs at once. They name the sound and they make it. "The bacon sizzled" tells you and lets you hear it. In the wait poem, "the tell-tale click of the door" ends on a sound you can almost hear. Click is short and sharp, like a real latch.

Sound is also built into softer tricks. Repeating the same first sound in a row of words, like "slow, slippery, slush," is called *alliteration*. It makes the line feel slick. A poet chooses sounds the way a cook chooses spices. Read the poem aloud and notice which sounds keep coming back. They are there for a reason.

words.d: a word that imitates a real noise, like buzz or crash; also called onomatopoeia
the same beginning sound repeated in words close together, like slow slippery slush

look.title: The Kitchen at Seven
look.text: A poem written for this lesson: "Sizzle of eggs, / clatter of plates, / the fridge door thunk, / the kettle's rising whistle, / and under it all / the hum." Read it aloud. Some words are noises. Some just describe.
look.prompt: Which words are sound words? Which one comes closest to the real noise? Which sound would you add?

check.q: Which word is a sound word?
check.why: Hiss sounds like the noise it names.

check.q: What is alliteration?
choices: The same beginning sound in words close together
A rhyme at the end of lines
check.why: Slow, slippery, slush all start with the same sound.

check.q: Why do poets use sound words?
choices: They are the only words allowed
They name a sound and make the sound at the same time
check.why: Sizzle tells you about bacon and lets you hear it.

lessons.title: Dickinson and Rossetti
lessons.mainIdea: Emily Dickinson and Christina Rossetti wrote short poems with plain words that still carry big feelings when you read them closely.
reading: "I'm nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?" That is how one of Emily Dickinson's most famous poems begins. Dickinson lived in Amherst, Massachusetts, in the 1800s. She rarely left her house and published almost nothing while she was alive. After she died in 1886, her family found hundreds of poems in her room.

Look at those two lines closely. Nobody is usually an insult. Dickinson turns it into a secret handshake: are you nobody too? Then we can be nobodies together. The words are tiny. The idea, that you do not have to be famous to matter, is not tiny at all. Reading closely means slowing down until you see that.

Christina Rossetti, an English poet born in 1830, wrote the wind poem you read earlier. Her poems for children are short and sound like songs. Both poets prove something worth knowing: a poem does not need long words or long lines. It needs the right words. When you read them, ask what each small word is doing. Usually it is doing a lot.

words.d: reading slowly and carefully, noticing what each word is doing
to print writing so other people can read it

look.title: Nobody Meets Nobody
look.text: I'm nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, opening lines of a poem written about 1861 and published in 1891
look.prompt: Why might the speaker be glad to meet another nobody? Is being nobody a bad thing in this poem?

check.q: What was unusual about Emily Dickinson's life as a poet?
choices: She published almost nothing while alive
check.why: Most of her poems were found after her death in 1886.

check.q: In "I'm nobody! Who are you?" how does Dickinson use the word nobody?
choices: As an insult to the reader
As a name for a monster
As a friendly secret shared with the reader
check.why: She turns nobody into a bond: we can be nobodies together.

check.q: What do Dickinson and Rossetti show about poems?
choices: Short, plain words can carry big ideas
check.why: Both used small words and short lines to say large things.

lessons.title: Stevenson and Dunbar
lessons.mainIdea: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote poems from a child's eye, and Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote poems full of music and feeling about freedom.
reading: "How do you like to go up in a swing, / Up in the air so blue?" Robert Louis Stevenson wrote that. He was born in Scotland in 1850. He also wrote the adventure book Treasure Island. As a boy he was sick a lot and spent long days in bed. Many of his poems for children are about what a kid sees from a bed, a window or a swing.

Paul Laurence Dunbar was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1872. His parents had been *enslaved*. He wrote poems while working as an elevator operator. He became one of the first Black American poets read all over the country. In 1893 he came to Chicago for the World's Fair. There he met Frederick Douglass.

Dunbar's poem Sympathy begins, "I know why the caged bird sings, ah me, / When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore." A bird in a cage *stands for* a person who is not free. Reading Dunbar closely means asking what the bird stands for. He died young, at 33. His lines are still read aloud today.

words.d: represents; a caged bird stands for a person who is not free
forced to work for someone as their property, with no freedom

look.title: The Caged Bird
look.text: I know why the caged bird sings, ah me, / When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore.
look.cite: Paul Laurence Dunbar, opening of Sympathy, 1899
look.prompt: What might the cage stand for? Why does the bird sing when it is hurt?

check.q: What are many of Stevenson's children's poems about?
choices: What a child sees from a bed, window or swing
check.why: Stevenson was sick as a boy and wrote from a child's eye view.

check.q: In Dunbar's Sympathy, the caged bird stands for
choices: a person who is not free
check.why: The bird in a cage represents someone denied freedom.

check.q: Which fact about Dunbar is true?
choices: His parents had been enslaved and he became a famous poet
check.why: Dunbar, born in Ohio to formerly enslaved parents, became a nationally read poet.

lessons.title: Reading a Script
lessons.mainIdea: A play is written as a script with a cast list, lines of dialogue, stage directions and scenes, and each part has a job.
reading: A play does not look like a story. It looks like this. CAST: RIDER, CHILD. SCENE 1: A window, night. Wind. CHILD: (pressing her face to the glass) Who is out there? RIDER: (from far off) Only me, and the storm. The words a character says come after the character's name. Everything else is instructions.

The list of characters at the top is the *cast*. The words after a name are that character's lines, the dialogue. The words in parentheses, like (pressing her face to the glass), are *stage directions*. They tell actors what to do, not what to say. You never read them out loud.

A play is cut into *scenes*. A new scene usually means a new place or a new time. "SCENE 2: The same window, morning." When you read a play alone, picture the stage. When you read it with others, each person takes a part. The story only exists when someone speaks the lines. That is the strange, great thing about a play.

words.d: the list of characters in a play
instructions in a script, often in parentheses, telling actors what to do
one part of a play, usually set in one place and time

look.title: A Very Short Scene
look.text: SCENE 1. A kitchen, morning. MOM: (holding up a dented fender) Which one of you wants to go first? ANDRE: (pointing) Him. JALEN: (at the same time, pointing) Him. MOM: (sitting down) Great. This should be quick.
look.cite: model script, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which words would you say aloud? Which would you only do? How do the stage directions make the scene funny?

check.q: What are stage directions?
choices: Instructions telling actors what to do, not read aloud
check.why: Words in parentheses tell actors what to do. They are not spoken.

check.q: What does a new scene usually mean?
check.why: Scenes divide a play by where and when it happens.

check.q: Where do you find a character's spoken lines in a script?
check.why: The character's name comes first, then the words that character says.

lessons.title: Reader's Theater
lessons.mainIdea: In reader's theater you read a script aloud with a group, using your voice to become the character, with no costumes or memorizing needed.
reading: Mr. Bell's class did not build a set or sew costumes. They pulled chairs into a half circle, took parts, and read the storm play out loud. That is *reader's theater*. You keep the script in your hands. Your voice does the acting. It is the easiest way to perform a play, and one of the best ways to get better at reading.

Your voice has tools. Volume: loud for the rider shouting over the wind, soft for the child at the window. Speed: fast when scared, slow when sleepy. *Tone*: the feeling in your voice, angry or kind or teasing. Read your line to yourself first, decide what the character feels, then say it that way.

Two habits make it work. Read your part more than once before the group starts. And listen to the others, so you come in on time. Kids who do reader's theater often read faster and smoother afterward, because they have practiced the same lines until the words feel like their own. Reading out loud with feeling is practice that does not feel like practice.

words.d: performing a play by reading the script aloud in a group, with voices instead of costumes
the feeling in a voice, such as angry, kind, scared or teasing

look.title: One Line, Four Ways
look.text: The line is: "Only me, and the storm." Say it as a tired old rider. Say it as a ghost. Say it as someone trying not to scare a small child. Say it as someone trying very hard to scare a small child.
look.prompt: What did you change each time: volume, speed or tone? Which version fits the poem best?

check.q: What do you use to act in reader's theater?
choices: Your voice, with the script in your hands
check.why: Reader's theater is reading aloud with feeling. No costumes or memorizing.

check.q: What is tone?
check.why: Tone is the emotion your voice carries: angry, kind, scared.

check.q: Why does reader's theater help students read better?
choices: They practice the same lines until the words feel like their own
There is no reading in it
check.why: Repeated reading with feeling builds speed and smoothness.

lessons.title: Poem, Story, Play
lessons.mainIdea: A poem, a story and a play can all tell about the same thing, but each form gives the reader something different.
reading: A rider gallops through a storm at night. Stevenson made it a poem: four short lines, a drumbeat, one picture. Mr. Bell's play made it two voices, a child and a rider, talking across the wind. A story could make it a whole chapter: who the rider is, where he is going, why the child cannot sleep. Same night, three *forms*.

Each form has strengths. A poem is short and musical, so it gives you a feeling fast. A story gives you time: characters, setting, a plot with a problem and a solution. A play gives you voices and puts you in the room. When you *compare* forms, ask: what can this one do that the others cannot?

Try it yourself. Take any small moment, like the first snow of the year in Illinois. As a poem it might be six lines about the hush. As a story it might be a kid who wakes up, sees white, and races to find her boots. As a play it might be two kids at a bus stop arguing about whether school will close. All three are true. Each one shows a different side.

words.d: the shape a piece of writing takes, such as a poem, a story or a play
to look at two or more things side by side and find what is the same and what is different

look.title: First Snow, Three Ways
look.text: Version one, a poem: six short lines about the hush when snow falls on a Chicago street at night. Version two, a story: a girl wakes up, sees white out the window, and tears the house apart looking for her boots. Version three, a play: two kids at a bus stop arguing about whether school will close.
look.prompt: Which version would you rather read? Which would you rather write? What does each form do that the others cannot?

check.q: What does a play give a reader that a poem usually does not?
choices: Different characters' voices speaking to each other
check.why: A play is built from dialogue between characters.

check.q: Which form usually gives the most time for characters, setting and plot?
check.why: A story has room to build characters and a full plot.

check.q: What does comparing three forms about the same thing show you?
choices: Each form shows a different side
check.why: Same moment, three forms, three different strengths.

review.why: The pattern of stressed syllables makes the galloping sound.

review.q: A line that repeats in a poem, like a chorus, is a
review.why: A refrain is a repeated line.

review.why: It makes you feel the heat through touch. That is imagery.

Which poet wrote the lines about the caged bird?
